note: The Roman government once sent two military officials to the Sages of Israel with an order: teach us your Torah. They read it through three times. As they left, they said they had examined the whole Torah and found it true, except for one rule: if a Jew's ox gores a gentile's ox the owner is exempt, but if a gentile's ox gores a Jew's ox he pays in full. Either the Torah's words of another apply only to Jews, and then the gentile should be exempt too, or they apply to everyone, and then the Jew should pay too. But they said they would not report this to the government.
why: The Sages tell this story in connection with the rule the officials challenge, the different treatment of a Jew's ox and a gentile's ox, which the Gemara has just been discussing.

terms.meaning: An innocuous ox has no record of goring and its owner pays half the damage; a forewarned ox has gored before and its owner pays in full.
Words from the Torah's law of goring oxen, about an ox that gores the ox of another person.

note: The daughter of Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda died. The Sages asked Ulla to come with them to console him, but he refused: the Babylonians console mourners by saying what can be done, which implies they would act against God's decree if they could, and he called that heresy. He went alone and spoke to the father about God telling Moses not to make war on Moab. Moses had reasoned that if the Torah ordered Israel to strike the Midianites, who only helped Moab, then surely Moab itself should be attacked. God answered that He had two good fledglings to bring out of them, Ruth the Moabite and Naamah the Ammonite. Ulla reasoned that if God spared two great nations for two such women, then if the daughter had been righteous and fit to bring good into the world, she would surely have lived.
why: The story is told in passing after the account of the Roman officials, and its mention of Moab and Ammon leads the Gemara on to a teaching that God rewards even refined speech.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
people.about: A Sage whose daughter died; Ulla calls him his teacher.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: He refuses the Babylonian form of consolation and goes alone to comfort the father.

people.name: Moses
people.about: In Ulla's words, he reasoned that Moab should be attacked and God stopped him.

people.name: Ruth the Moabite
people.about: Named by God as one of the two good fledglings for whose sake Moab was spared.

people.name: Naamah the Ammonite
people.about: Named by God as the other good fledgling, for whose sake Ammon was spared.

terms.meaning: An argument from a lesser case to a greater one: if this is true here, it is all the more true there.
Neighboring peoples who, in the Torah, joined against Israel in the wilderness.

note: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel applied the verse "My eye affected my soul, because of all the daughters of my city" to his own family: there were a thousand children in his father's household, five hundred studying Torah and five hundred studying Greek wisdom, and the only ones left were himself and his cousin in Asia Minor. The Sages explained that Rabban Gamliel's household was different because it was close to the government, just as they allowed Avtolmos bar Reuven, who was also close to the government, to cut his hair in the Roman style.
why: The Gemara has cited a curse on anyone who teaches his son Greek wisdom; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's account seems to show it was studied freely in his father's house, and the Sages explain why that family was an exception.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: He tells of the thousand children in his father's household, of whom only he and a cousin remained.

people.name: Avtolmos bar Reuven
people.about: A man close to the government who was allowed to wear the Roman-style haircut.

terms.meaning: Greek learning and culture, which the Sages restricted at a time of war with Rome.
A Roman hairstyle; adopting it was treated as following the ways of the gentiles.
Gentile customs that the Torah forbids Jews to imitate.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core text the Gemara discusses.

note: Rabbi Yirmeya's brother-in-law, a minor, shut the doors of his late father's house against Rabbi Yirmeya, who claimed part of it. Rabbi Yirmeya took the case to Rabbi Avin, who said the boy was holding what was his. Rabbi Yirmeya offered witnesses that he had taken possession while the father was alive, but Rabbi Avin said testimony is not accepted in the absence of the other party, and a minor cannot stand as one. Rabbi Yirmeya protested: had the whole world lined up behind Sumakhos to take away what was his? The case reached Rabbi Abbahu, who cited a ruling that land a child seizes is taken from him at once, and he may bring witnesses when he grows up. The Gemara rejects that comparison, since this boy inherited the house; the text does not say how the case ended.
why: The Gemara has just cited a teaching on whether minor heirs must return what their father stole, with Sumakhos disagreeing; this case turns on that dispute and leads into a discussion of testimony given when a party is absent.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: He claims a share of his father-in-law's house and is shut out by his young brother-in-law.

people.name: Rabbi Avin
people.about: The judge who first hears the case and favors the boy.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: The Sage the case finally reaches; he cites a ruling in Rabbi Yirmeya's favor.

people.name: Sumakhos
people.about: An early Sage who held that minor heirs are exempt; Rabbi Avin points to his view.

terms.meaning: A child under the age of legal adulthood, who cannot be a party to a court case.
A legal assumption that whoever holds property, here by inheriting it, owns it unless proven otherwise.

note: A man from Naresh stole a scroll and sold it to a man from Pappunya for eighty dinars, who sold it on to a man from Mehoza for one hundred and twenty. Then the thief was identified. Abaye ruled that the owner should pay the man from Mehoza eighty dinars and take back his scroll, and the man from Mehoza should collect the other forty from the man from Pappunya. Rava objected and ruled instead that the owner pays the full one hundred and twenty, then collects forty from the man from Pappunya and eighty from the thief from Naresh.
why: The Gemara is working through cases of the Sages' ordinance that an owner pays to reclaim stolen goods from an innocent buyer; this case asks how it applies when the item passes through a second buyer.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: He gives the first ruling on how the payments should be divided.

people.name: Rava
people.about: He objects to Abaye and gives a different division.

terms.meaning: An ordinance of the Sages: an owner who reclaims stolen goods from an innocent buyer repays the buyer's price, so that people are not afraid to buy in the market.
